assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation (BLP) and the Ericson-Pakes framework for dynamic industry models made empirical industrial organisation and adjacent fields (trade, health, environment, antitrust practice) workable with realistic substitution patterns and market dynamics. The methodological reach is broad and well beyond one subfield.
assessment.attribution: Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes (1995) is the clear centre for demand estimation, with Pakes' further work on dynamic games and the Berry (1994) inversion. Bresnahan, Benkard, Reiss and Levin made important contributions but are less central to this specific discovery. Limiting the award to three names omits real contributors.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use, extensive replication across applications and wide adoption in regulatory and merger analysis. Timing is no obstacle.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would rather credit Bresnahan or Reiss for earlier empirical IO foundations.
My recollection of relative credit within the broader structural-IO group is not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a tractable, uniquely solved non-cooperative foundation for bargaining and linked it to market outcomes through the Rubinstein-Wolinsky decentralised-trade models. It is a core building block in game theory, labour, industrial organisation and matching and market-design theory.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the central, uncontested contribution. Wolinsky's work on bargaining in markets is a distinct and cited extension. Binmore's contributions (including the Binmore-Rubinstein-Wolinsky link to Nash bargaining) are real but more of a supporting and interpretive character.
assessment.maturity: More than four decades of confirmation and use, with abundant evidence of lasting influence. Maturity is not in doubt.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer a single laureate or Rubinstein with Wolinsky.
Weighing Binmore's role against Wolinsky's, which is a judgment call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) showed how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks, creating a durable framework for credit cycles that underlies much later macro-finance and policy analysis, including work after 2008.
assessment.attribution: The collateral-credit-cycle mechanism is cleanly credited to Kiyotaki and Moore. The financial-accelerator strand (Bernanke-Gertler, Gilchrist) is related but partly overlaps with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, so I confine the proposal to the two core authors.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of influence and extensive empirical and quantitative development, including in policy institutions. Mature.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises, which could reduce the committee's appetite.
Whether Gertler and Gilchrist should be included to reflect the financial accelerator.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Sticky-price and sticky-wage microfoundations, the New Keynesian synthesis and rule-based monetary policy underpin modern central-bank practice. The impact on both theory and policy is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: This is the hardest candidate to attribute, since the field has many contributors (Calvo, Taylor, Rotemberg, Woodford, Galí, Clarida, Gertler, Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans, Smets-Wouters) and the longlist names eight. Any three-person selection is partly arbitrary and risks leaving out major figures.
assessment.maturity: Mature with decades of confirmation, though some recent critiques (HANK, post-2021 inflation) are ongoing. That does not weaken the foundational contribution.
uncertainties: Attribution is genuinely contested and the three-name cap forces exclusions.
Rotemberg and Clarida do not appear in the credited names, so the list is incomplete.
Recent inflation experience may be read as either vindicating or challenging the framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models (Melitz 2003; Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple) shifted the unit of analysis from industries to firms, explaining selection, exporter premia and the new margins of gains from trade. They generated a large empirical literature.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the central author of the selection model, with Helpman as an architect of the broader new trade theory and heterogeneous-firm extensions. Redding, Bernard, Eaton and Kortum contributed to the wider field. Bernard and Eaton do not appear in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation and extension. It is sufficiently mature, though the Krugman prize in 2008 covered adjacent ground.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2008 prize and with the quantitative trade candidate.
Several key contributors to the firm-level trade literature are not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion gives a clean, general framework for how a sender can optimally shape information, with uses in regulation, disclosure, advertising, auctions and mechanism and market design. The conceptual contribution is high.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica-Gentzkow (2011) is the central paper. Bergemann and Morris developed related information-design and robust-mechanism work. The line between persuasion and information design makes the credit more diffuse than the three-name cap allows.
assessment.maturity: Roughly fifteen years old. Influence is very large in theory, but empirical confirmation and downstream real-world impact are still developing, so timing is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Whether Bergemann and Morris should be included for information design.
Whether the field has matured enough relative to older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and policy-relevant causal estimates, and it set a new standard for empirical public and labour economics.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader of the programme, with Hendren and Friedman as key co-authors. Katz is credited for earlier mobility and Moving to Opportunity work. Team-based research makes individual attribution less clear than for a single-idea theory prize.
assessment.maturity: Highly influential but most of the work is from the last decade, and some findings (for example neighbourhood and causal-mechanism claims) are still being replicated and debated.
uncertainties: Early relative to the core theory and methods candidates.
Contribution is partly a data and measurement advance, and its durability is not yet fully established.
Overlap with credibility-revolution prizes in 2019 and 2021.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Double/debiased machine learning, causal forests and related methods enable valid inference on treatment effects in high-dimensional settings and have been taken up across economics and beyond.
assessment.attribution: Athey, Chernozhukov and Wager are all credited with distinct strands (heterogeneous effects, debiased ML). Chernozhukov's co-authors on double ML (Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey, Robins) are not listed, which makes attribution incomplete. Wager is relatively junior.
assessment.maturity: Mostly post-2015 work. Adoption is rapid but long-run durability relative to the 2021 prize on causal inference is not yet clear.
uncertainties: Early for a prize, and possibly seen as an extension of the 2021 causal-inference recognition.
Incomplete credited names for double ML.
Athey also appears in the digital-markets candidate, so credit may be split across lists.
